excerpt: Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions. We propose a lightweight method that detects CS directly from speech. It uses frame-level language information in pretrained speechâ¦

excerpt:
AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.

Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly).

I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development:

Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...]

This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[

With console makers go

# v0.31.0

## Highlights

This release features 717 commits from 307 contributors (96 new)!

* **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash performance**: FlashMLA mega attention with the V4.1 NVFP4 compressed KV cache is now the SM100 default (#56935); DeepGEMM sparse MQA logits for the indexer (#56254) and Mega-Gate fusing the gate GEMM with expert selection (#56266); decoder boundaries fuse the TP all-reduce, mHC input preparation (#57643) and the MoE finalize (#58586); a fused small-batch WO-A with inverse RoPE and MXFP8 quant on SM100/SM103 (#58634); the MXFP8 `wo_b` GEMM fused with the sequence-parallel reduce-scatter (#57428); Engram `wkv` sharded across TP ranks (#58678) and Engram host tables shared across co-located DP replicas by default (#57651); encoder CUDA graphs for the vision tower (#56625); and SWA bounded replay that keeps the sliding-window KV out of prefix caching (#56227).
* **Fast restart**: the new `vllm preload` CLI launches the weight-cache daemon that keeps post-quantized weights resident in GPU memory across engine restarts (#56680), now with data parallelism (#57386), MTP draft models (#57312), a `/health` endpoint (#58552) and a readiness wait (#58370). As we’re still in the early days of building applications with foundation models, it’s normal to make mistakes. This is a quick note with examples of some of the most common pitfalls that I’ve seen, both from public case studies and from my personal experience.

Because these pitfalls are common, if you’ve worked on any AI product, you’ve probably seen them before.

1. Use generative AI when you don't need generative AI

Every time there’s a new technology, I can hear the collective sigh of senior engineers everywhere: “Not everything is a nail.” Generative AI isn’t an exception — its seemingly limitless capabilities only exacerbate the tendency to use generative AI for everything.

A team pitched me the idea of using generative AI to optimize energy consumption. They fed a household’s list of energy-intensive activities and hourly electricity prices into an LLM, then asked it to create a schedule to minimize energy costs.
